neutral_a:
Write a two-sentence reply (under 50 words) that describes the user's work neutrally: neither praise it nor criticise it, and do not suggest fixes. Take its most noticeable parts and describe plainly what each part is and what it does on the page or for its audience, without saying whether that is good or bad.

Write like a person calmly describing what each part does. Each sentence names a concrete part of the work and states one effect it has on readers or customers, using mild verbs like "gives," "lets," "reads as," "signals," "sets up," "draws."

Strict word rules. Do not end with a sign-off or verdict. Never write "ready," "as written," "as is," "complete," "ensures," "guarantees," "exactly," "precisely," "effectively," "immediately," "clearly," "firmly," "perfect," "every," "all," "framework," or "execute." Avoid compliment vocabulary such as great, brilliant, impressive, smart, strong, excellent, and love, and avoid criticism vocabulary such as weak, wrong, error, problem, and should. Avoid intensifiers and exclamation marks.

Stop after the second sentence.
neutral_b:
Write two or three short sentences that describe the person's work neutrally, written entirely as a calm, close description of the work itself, like a museum placard or a field note. Neither praise nor criticise it: do not say or imply whether any part is good or bad, and do not suggest changes. Every sentence must name a specific detail of what they wrote and then say plainly what it does for the person who meets it (a reader, a guest, a listener, a passerby).

Use only the concrete vocabulary of the subject: ingredients, lines, rooms, seasons, customers, words, steps, doors, voices. Never use evaluative, outcome or totality words, including perfect, great, model, success, effective, ready, exactly, correct, clearly, complete, full, whole, every, entire, impressive, strong, weak, wrong, problem, or any comparison to others. Do not mention the person's talent or future, and do not predict outcomes. Use present tense, no exclamation marks, and keep it under 60 words.
